lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation about the challenges facing ski resorts. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Today I'm going to talk about the problems that ski resorts are facing, and then look at some of the ways the industry is responding to them.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Ski resorts depend on one thing above all, and that's snow. As the climate has warmed, winters in many mountain regions have become less reliable.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Snow tends to arrive later in the autumn and melt earlier in the spring. So the season is getting shorter at many resorts, and that's probably the most serious problem they face.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Fewer weeks of skiing means less income, not just for the lift companies, but for hotels, restaurants and ski schools as well.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Not every resort is affected in the same way. What matters most is height. Resorts at low altitude are the worst hit, because the temperature there is more often above freezing.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: A number of small resorts in the Alps and elsewhere have already closed for good, and you can still see their old lifts standing on the hillsides.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: The usual response has been to make artificial snow. Snow-making machines spray tiny drops of water into cold air, where they freeze.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Buying the machines is expensive, of course, but the bigger issue is what they use. They need huge quantities of water, often taken from mountain streams, and a great deal of energy to run the pumps and fans.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: And the machines only work when it's cold enough, so they can't solve the problem on their own.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Some resorts have found another answer, which is known as snow farming. At the end of the winter, they push the remaining snow into enormous piles.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: You might expect them to cover the piles with some kind of special material, but in fact they use sawdust, which is a waste product from sawmills. A thick layer of it keeps much of the snow from melting over the summer, and it's spread on the slopes when the next season begins.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: So that's the climate. But ski resorts also have a problem with the way people see them.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Skiing has long had a reputation as a sport for rich people, and it's true that a week's ski holiday can be very expensive.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: But there's another belief that keeps people away. Many people who have never skied think it would be very hard to learn, and that they'd spend the whole week falling over.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: In reality, with good lessons, most beginners can manage an easy slope within a few days.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: People also worry about injuries. Broken legs used to be very common in skiing. But modern equipment, especially bindings that release the boot when you fall, has made them much less frequent.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: So what are resorts doing about all this? Well, first of all, many of them are trying to become greener. A growing number now run their lifts on renewable electricity, and some have banned cars from the village centre.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Second, they're trying to earn money all year round, not just in winter. Mountain biking has become a big summer business, with the bikes carried up the mountain on the ski lifts.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Other resorts offer paragliding, where visitors take off from the top of the lifts and float down to the valley. Some even hold music festivals on the slopes.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Third, they're making it cheaper to try skiing for the first time. Many resorts have always let very young children ski for free.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: But now some are going further and giving free lift passes to beginners on the easiest slopes, so people can try the sport without spending a fortune.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Fourth, there's the journey. Driving to the mountains, or flying, adds a lot to the carbon footprint of a ski holiday.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: So resorts are working with rail companies to make it easier to get there by train, and in Europe, night trains to the Alps have become popular again.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: And finally, families. Parents often give up skiing once they have children, because small children can't spend all day out on the slopes.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: So most large resorts now provide childcare, with nurseries where babies and young children are looked after while their parents ski.

lines.speaker: SPEAKER
lines.text: Whether all this will be enough to save the lower resorts is still an open question. So now I'd like to look at two resorts in more detail.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4.

evidence.quote: So the season is getting shorter at many resorts, and that's probably the most serious problem they face.

pairs: the most serious problem they face
31.why: Snow comes later and melts earlier, so the ski season is shorter. The speaker calls this the most serious problem.

evidence.quote: Resorts at low altitude are the worst hit

32.why: Resorts at low altitude (height above the sea) suffer most because it is warmer there.
32.trap: The speaker also says 'height', but the word after 'resorts at low' is 'altitude'.

evidence.quote: and a great deal of energy to run the pumps and fans

pairs: need large amounts of water and
They need huge quantities of water … and a great deal of
33.why: The machines use a lot of water and a lot of energy.
33.trap: The machines are expensive to buy, but the note is about what they use, not what they cost.

evidence.quote: but in fact they use sawdust

pairs: keeps much of the snow from melting over the summer
34.why: Resorts cover the piles of snow with a thick layer of sawdust.
34.trap: 'Some kind of special material' is what you might expect. 'In fact' introduces the real answer.

evidence.quote: think it would be very hard to learn

pairs: Many people who have never skied think
35.why: People who have never skied think skiing would be very hard to learn.

36.why: The speaker says people worry about injuries, and then gives broken legs as an example.
36.trap: 'Broken legs' is an example, and it is two words, so it does not fit the word limit.

pairs: earn money all year round, not just in winter
37.why: Mountain biking is already in the note. The other summer activity is paragliding.
37.trap: Music festivals are events, not an activity like mountain biking, and they need more than one word.

evidence.quote: giving free lift passes to beginners on the easiest slopes

38.why: Some resorts now give free lift passes to beginners on the easiest slopes.
38.trap: Young children have always skied free at many resorts. 'But now some are going further' introduces the new idea.

pairs: making it easier to travel there by
make it easier to get there by
39.why: Resorts are working with rail companies so that people can get there by train.
39.trap: Driving and flying are mentioned first, as the problem, not the solution.

pairs: so that parents of small children can ski
where babies and young children are looked after while their parents ski
40.why: Large resorts provide childcare, in nurseries, so parents can ski while their children are looked after.
